extracted.intended_audience: Federal regulators, conservation biologists, land managers, and public commenters participating in ESA listing/delisting rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytical standards for evaluating whether a species should be delisted under the U.S. Endangered Species Act, including the SSA approach, threat evaluation, metrics of viability (resiliency/redundancy/representation), foreseeable future determinations, and monitoring/recovery considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4 statutory factors (A–E) for listing/delisting
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act requires that we determine whether any species is an endangered species or a threatened species because of any of the following factors: (A) The present or threatened destruction, modification, or curtailment of its habitat or range; (B) Overutilization for commercial, recreational, scientific, or educational purposes; (C) Disease or predation; (D) The inadequacy of existing regulatory mechanisms; or (E) Other natural or manmade factors affecting its continued existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five broad categories are the required analytical axes for deciding whether a species meets the statutory definition of endangered or threatened; the determination to delist must be based on an analysis of these same factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'threat'
rubrics_metrics.description: We use the term 'threat' to refer in general to actions or conditions that are known to or are reasonably likely to negatively affect individuals of a species. The term 'threat' includes actions or conditions that have a direct impact on individuals (direct impacts), as well as those that affect individuals through alteration of their habitat or required resources (stressors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threats may encompass either the source of the action/condition or the action/condition itself; identification of threats alone does not mean statutory listing criteria are met — their expected effects on individuals, populations, and the species must be evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threat evaluation and cumulative analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether a species meets the definition of 'endangered' or 'threatened', we must evaluate all identified threats by considering the species' expected response and the effects of the threats—in light of those actions and conditions that will ameliorate the threats—on an individual, population, and species level. We evaluate each threat and its expected effects on the species, then analyze the cumulative effect of all of the threats on the species as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cumulative analysis must also consider positive actions/conditions (e.g., regulatory mechanisms, conservation efforts) that ameliorate threats; only after this cumulative analysis does the Secretary determine status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreseeable future determination framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The foreseeable future extends as far into the future as the Services can make reasonably reliable predictions about the threats to the species and the species' responses to those threats. The Services need not identify the foreseeable future in terms of a specific period of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The foreseeable future is described case-by-case using best available data and considering factors such as the species' life-history characteristics, threat-projection timeframes, and environmental variability. 'Reliable' means sufficient to provide a reasonable degree of confidence in the prediction, not certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of best scientific and commercial data
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination to revise the status of a species is ultimately based on an analysis of the best scientific and commercial data available to determine whether a species is no longer an endangered or threatened species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SSA and rulemaking analyses rely on the best available information (including recent peer-reviewed publications and monitoring data); new or recent data (e.g., taxonomic/genetic studies) constitute the best available information even if online databases lag in recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viability principles: resiliency, redundancy, and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: To assess species viability we used the three conservation biology principles of resiliency, redundancy, and representation (Shaffer and Stein 2000). Resiliency is the ability of the species to withstand environmental and demographic stochasticity; redundancy is the ability to withstand catastrophic events; and representation is the ability to adapt to near-term and long-term changes in the environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Species viability generally increases with increases in these three principles. The SSA identifies ecological requirements at individual, population (AU), and species levels and describes risk and beneficial factors influencing viability using these principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: SSA three-stage analytical process
rubrics_metrics.description: The SSA process is categorized into three sequential stages: (1) evaluate individual species' life-history needs; (2) assess historical and current condition of demographics and habitat characteristics, including how species arrived at current condition; (3) make predictions about species' responses to positive and negative environmental and anthropogenic influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout these stages the best available information is used to characterize viability as the ability to sustain populations in the wild over time; the SSA provides the scientific basis informing regulatory decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: AU (analysis unit) resiliency requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To be sufficiently resilient, populations (AUs) require survivorship and recruitment at rates that are able to sustain AUs, in addition to pollinator connectivity between individuals and clusters of plants within the AU. Adequately resilient AUs also contain enough individuals across each life stage (seed, seedling, mature reproductive adult) to bounce back after experiencing environmental stressors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resiliency evaluation uses multiple metrics (see resiliency scoring metrics) to assess whether AUs meet these demographic and connectivity thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundancy requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of AUs across the landscape influence redundancy; more AUs across the range increase each species' ability to withstand catastrophic events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AUs are delineated by natural geological and ecological features and management boundaries; redundancy assessment considers spatial distribution and number of sufficiently resilient AUs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals and AUs inhabiting diverse ecological settings and exhibiting genetic or phenological variation add to representation across the species' ranges. The greater diversity in genetics, habitats, and morphology, the more likely the species can adapt to change over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation assessment examines genetic analyses, habitat diversity, and phenological variation across AUs to determine adaptive capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stressors with potential AU- or species-level effects (list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stressors that have the potential to present AU-level effects for both species include livestock use, invasive species, oil and gas development, OHV recreational use, development and maintenance of utility corridors, and the effects of global climate change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other identified stressors (e.g., predation, herbicides, pesticides, collection/commercial trade) were considered but determined not to have species- or AU-level effects, and thus were not addressed in resiliency analysis in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threat inclusion threshold for resiliency analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Only threats that had the potential now or in the future to have AU- or species-level effects to either species were included in the resiliency analysis. Threats limited in magnitude that impact only individual plants were not included as AU- or species-level threats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This threshold explains excluding issues like limited collection or localized predation from the broader resiliency scoring when their magnitude is insufficient to affect populations or species viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resiliency scoring metrics (habitat condition index and water deficit metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: We evaluated the effects of stressors that impact biological soil crusts as part of the habitat condition index metric in our SSA report. We evaluated water availability during the growing season with a water deficit metric. These two metrics provide two of the four scores in the current and future resiliency evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct data on some factors (e.g., biological soil crusts) are lacking, related measurements (bare ground, native/invasive cover) are used; resiliency scoring is multi-metric and uses best available proxies where direct measures are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and evaluation of land-management designations as conservation mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximately 30 percent of the land in S. glaucus AUs and 41 percent of the land in S. dawsoniae AUs have BLM designations (NCAs, ACECs, WSA, Wilderness Area) that limit or exclude authorization of certain land uses. These protections are not contingent upon Federal listing status and help to facilitate maintenance and recovery of cactus occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments consider how these designations reduce specific stressors; the presence and specific protections of ACECs/NCAs/WSAs are used as ameliorating factors in the cumulative threat analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring adequacy for post-delisting monitoring (PDM) and rangewide trend detection
rubrics_metrics.description: The PDM plan relies on the sampling protocols used in Krening et al. (2021a), which are sufficient to detect rangewide trends for both species. BLM will provide information on newly approved, permitted, or implemented projects and impacts to Colorado hookless cactus on an annual basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PDM plan identifies potential actions if monitoring indicates substantial decline (meet with partners, extend monitoring period, modify monitoring practices, initiate rangewide status assessment, or relist), and will be refined collaboratively with partners to ensure appropriate duration and detection ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for excluding non-motorized recreation as a stressor
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-motorized recreation (mountain bikes, hiking, camping, etc.) was not included in the resiliency evaluation due to the relatively small footprint and localized impacts of these activities, BLM's general avoidance of Colorado hookless cactus when designing non-motorized trail routes, and the lack of species- or AU-level effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion is justified when footprint, management avoidance, and lack of evidence for broader impacts indicate no measurable AU- or species-level effect; commenters must provide specific evidence to the contrary for reconsideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of difficult-to-detect ecological factors (e.g., biological soil crusts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biological soil crusts (BSCs) may be difficult to detect and the best available information within the species' range identifies bare ground and native/invasive plant cover but no direct information on BSCs. The commenter did not provide additional information linking BSCs to population-level effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct measures are absent, related indicators (bare ground, plant cover) are evaluated and stressors that affect those indicators are incorporated into broader habitat condition metrics used in the SSA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of analysis units (AUs) as population delineations
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of analysis in the SSA report, the ranges were divided into analysis units (AUs). AUs, synonymous with populations, include many cactus individuals and were delineated by natural geological and ecological features and management boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AU-level analyses enable evaluation of resiliency per population, and aggregate AU outcomes inform redundancy and representation conclusions at the species level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery plan requirements and role of recovery outlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 4(f)(1)(B)(ii), recovery plans must, to the maximum extent practicable, include objective, measurable criteria which, when met, would result in a determination that the species be removed from the Lists. Recovery plans provide a roadmap but are not regulatory documents and do not substitute for determinations under section 4(a)(1) of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a full recovery plan is not prepared (e.g., due to staff capacity), a recovery outline may be used to present preliminary recovery strategy and actions; recovery is dynamic and may be achieved without fully meeting every recovery-plan criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for considering new scientific information (e.g., genetic/taxonomic studies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent peer-reviewed genetic analyses and official species descriptions (e.g., McGlaughlin and Naibauer 2023/2024) constitute the best available scientific information for drafting the rule, even if other databases (e.g., NatureServe) have not yet updated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory analysis incorporates newly published peer-reviewed results; absence of database recognition does not preclude using published, peer-reviewed, best-available science in status determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Livestock grazing impact assessment and management tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderate to heavy domestic livestock grazing has been observed to cause physical damage (trampling) to Sclerocactus plants on rare occasions; overgrazing can facilitate invasive species like cheatgrass. BLM management plans allow stipulations in grazing permits (reductions, timing/duration adjustments) to benefit natural resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment weighs observed impacts, potential for facilitating invasives, and available BLM management mechanisms to limit harmful grazing effects; absence of evidence for widespread illegal grazing in the species' range affects inclusion in the SSA.
